title: De Natura Rerum Ad Sisebestum Regem Liber
author: Isidorus Hispalensis
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1422.tmp1422.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: 1. Sicut ait Ambrosius, tempora sunt vices mutationum, in quibus sol certa cursus sui dimensione anni orbem diffusa varietate distinguit. Tempora autem motos siderum sunt. Unde et Deus, cum hæc institueret, dixit : Et sint in signa, et tempora, et dies, et annos, id est, in aliquo mutabili motu, cujus aliud prius, aliud posterius fraeterit, eo quod simul esse non possint.
passages.english: 1. As Ambrose says, times are the successions of changes, in which the sun, by the fixed measure of its course, marks off the circle of the year with a widespread variety. Times, moreover, are the motions of the stars. Hence God too, when he established these things, said: "And let them be for signs, and for times, and for days, and for years", that is, in some changeable motion, of which one part passes first and another later, because they cannot exist at the same time.
passages.notes: "fraeterit" read as "praeterit" (passes).

passages.original: 1. In definitione autem mundi circulos aiunt philosophi quinque, quos Graeci zonas vocant, in quibus dividitur orbis terrae. 17 Has Virgilius in Georgicis ostendit, dicens : Quinque tenent cœlum zonae. Sed fingamus eas in modum dexterae nostrae, ut Pollet sit circulus Arcticus, frigore inhabitabilis; secundus circulus Therinus, temperatus habitabilis; medius circulus Isemerinus, torridus inhabitabilis;
passages.english: 1. In describing the world, the philosophers speak of five circles, which the Greeks call zones, into which the circle of the earth is divided. Virgil points these out in the Georgics, saying: "Five zones hold the sky." But let us picture them after the manner of our right hand, so that the thumb is the Arctic circle, uninhabitable because of cold; the second, the Therinus [summer] circle, temperate and habitable; the middle, the Isemerinus [equinoctial] circle, torrid and uninhabitable;
passages.notes: "Pollet" read as "pollex" (thumb). The stray "17" is a footnote or column mark and is omitted.

passages.original: Solstitialis vero circulus, qui in Oriente inter septentrionalem et æstivum est collocatus, et iste qui in Occidente inter aestivum et australem est positus, ideo temperati sunt, quod ex uno circulo rigorem, ex altero calorem habeant. De quibus Virgilius : Has inter, mediamque duae mortalibus aegris Munere concessas divum. 18 Sed qui proximi sunt æstive circulo, ipsi sunt Æthiopes nimio calore perusti.
passages.english: The solstitial circle, which in the East is placed between the northern and the summer [circle], and the one which in the West is set between the summer and the southern, are temperate for this reason: that they have cold from one circle and heat from the other. Of these Virgil [says]: "Between these and the middle one, two are granted to wretched mortals by the gift of the gods." But those who are nearest to the summer circle are the Ethiopians, scorched by excessive heat.
passages.notes: The stray "18" is a footnote mark and is omitted. The geometry of the passage is confused as transmitted.

passages.original: 2. De coeli autem nomine sic dicit sanctus Ambrosius in libris quos scripsit de creatione mundi : Cælum Græco vocabulo ούρανός, dicitur; apud Latinos autem propterea cœlum appellatur, quia impressa stellarum lumina, veluti signa, habens, tanquam cælatum dicitur, sicut argentum, quod signis eminentibus refulget, cœlatum vocatur.
passages.english: 2. Concerning the name of the sky, Saint Ambrose speaks thus in the books he wrote on the creation of the world: The sky is called by the Greek word ouranos; among the Latins, however, it is called caelum because, having the lights of the stars impressed on it like engraved figures, it is said to be as it were caelatum [engraved], just as silver that gleams with raised figures is called caelatum.

passages.original: 3. Partes autem ejus: chous, axis, cardines, convela, poli,sidera.Chous, quod coelum continet. Unde Ennius : Vix solum complere choum terroribus caeli. Axis, linea recta, quae per mediam pilam sphæræ tendit. Cardines, extremæ axis partes sunt. Convexa, 22 extrema coeli. Poli, ex coelestibus circulis cacumina, quibus maxime sphaera nititur : quorum alter ad Aquilonem spectans Boreus, alter terrae oppositus Austronotus dictus est.
passages.english: 3. Its parts are these: the *chous*, the axis, the hinges, the vaults, the poles, the stars. The *chous* is that which contains the sky; hence Ennius: "Scarcely to fill the ground and the *chous* with the terrors of the sky." The axis is the straight line that runs through the middle of the ball of the sphere. The hinges are the extreme parts of the axis. The vaults are the outer limits of the sky. The poles are the summits of the heavenly circles, on which the sphere chiefly rests: of these, the one facing the north is called Boreus, the other, opposite the earth, is called Austronotus.
passages.notes: "chous" (Greek-derived, apparently from cohum/chaos) is an obscure word for the vault containing the sky; kept untranslated. The list has "convela", evidently a scanning error for "convexa", as the following definition shows. "22" is a page or footnote number and is omitted. The Ennius line is obscure and the text uncertain.

passages.original: Duo sunt autem, ut diximus, poli, quibus coelum volvitur, Boreus, quem Aquilonium vocamus. Iiic Arcti, id est, septentriones, qui nobis semper apparent. Cui contrarius est Notius qui australis dicitur. Hic est, qui terra, ut ait Cicero, tegitur, et 23 ὰϕανής a Graecis nominatur. Tanta autem polus celeritate ferri dicitur, ut nisi adversus ejus præcipitem cursum astra currant, mundi ruinam faciant. Fertur enim ejus preceps volubilitas cursu siderum temperari. Unde Lucanus : Sideribus quae sola fugam moderantur olympi, Occurruntque polo, diversa potentia prima Mundi lege data est.
passages.english: There are, as we have said, two poles on which the sky turns: the Boreus, which we call the Aquilonian [northern]. Here are the Arcti, that is, the Septentriones [the Bears], which always appear to us. Opposite to it is the Notius, which is called the southern. This is the one which, as Cicero says, is covered by the earth, and is named aphanēs [invisible] by the Greeks. The pole is said to be carried with such speed that, unless the stars ran against its headlong course, they would bring about the ruin of the world. For its headlong rotation is said to be tempered by the course of the stars. Hence Lucan: "To the stars which alone check the flight of Olympus and run against the pole, a contrary power was given by the first law of the world."
passages.notes: "Iiic" read as "Hic". The stray "23" is a footnote mark and is omitted.

passages.original: 1. Ambrosius sanctus, in libro Hexaemeron sic loquitur, dicens : Legimus in Davia: Laudate eum cœli cœlorum. Utrum enim unum sit coelum an plures, contentio est, dum aliqui multos esse 24 asserunt, alii autem, præter unum, alios esse negant. Philosophi autem mundi septem cœlos, id est, planetarum globos consono motu introduxerunt.
passages.english: 1. Saint Ambrose, in the book Hexaemeron, speaks thus, saying: We read in David: "Praise him, you heavens of heavens." For whether there is one heaven or several is a matter of dispute, since some assert that there are many, while others deny that there are any besides the one. But the philosophers of the world introduced seven heavens, that is, the spheres of the planets, with harmonious motion.
passages.notes: "Davia" read as "David". The stray "24" is a footnote mark and is omitted.

passages.original: 1. Dicunt antiqui, Aratus et Hyginus, solem per seipsum moveri, non cum mundo verti uno loco manentem. Nam si fixus maneret, necesse erat eodem loco occidere et exoriri a quo pridie fuerat exortus, quemadmodum caetera siderum signa oriuntur et occidunt.
passages.english: 1. The ancients, Aratus and Hyginus, say that the sun moves by itself, and does not turn with the world while remaining in one place. For if it remained fixed, it would necessarily set and rise in the same place from which it had risen the day before, just as the other constellations of the stars rise and set.

passages.original: 1. Ait Sanctus Augustinus in Psalmi decimi expositione : < Quaeritur, inquit, unde habet luna tumen. Duæ tantum opiniones traduntur, sed quae sit harum verax, duhium fertur quemquam scire posse. Alii namque dicunt proprium eam lumen habere, globique ejus unam partem esse lucifluam , aliam vero obscuram, et dum movetur in circulo suo, eamdem partem, qua lucet, paulatim ad terras converti, ut videri a nobis possit, et ideo prius quasi corniculato lumine fulget.
passages.english: 1. Saint Augustine says in the exposition of the tenth Psalm: "It is asked," he says, "where the moon has its light from. Only two opinions are handed down, but which of these is true, it is said to be doubtful that anyone can know. For some say that it has its own light, and that one part of its globe is light-giving and the other dark, and that as it moves in its circle, the same part with which it shines is gradually turned toward the earth, so that it can be seen by us, and therefore it first shines with a sort of horned light.
passages.notes: "tumen" read as "lumen" and "duhium" as "dubium".

passages.original: Constat ergo lunam ex solis radiis lumen accipere, et dum objectu terrae solem non aspexeril, tunc lumen amittere. Nam dicunt stoici omnem terram montibus claudi, quorum umbra fertur luna subito non apparere. Unde Lucanus: Jam Phœbe totum fratri cum reddere! orbem' Terrarum subila percussa expalluit umbra.
passages.english: It is clear, therefore, that the moon receives its light from the rays of the sun, and loses its light when, through the interposition of the earth, it does not see the sun. For the Stoics say that the whole earth is enclosed by mountains, and that through their shadow the moon is said suddenly not to appear. Hence Lucan: "Now when Phoebe was returning her whole orb to her brother, struck by the sudden shadow of the earth, she grew pale."
passages.notes: "aspexeril" read as "aspexerit" and "subila" as "subita". The stray marks in the Lucan quotation are omitted.

passages.original: Sexto Pha et hontis stellam, quam Jutis appellant. Jam summo cœlo, id est in mundi vertice, stella Saturni est posita , quæ quidcm dum summum coelum teneat, sublimiorque sit omnibus, natura tamen ejus frigida fertur, approbante Virgilio: Frigida Saturni sese quo stella receptet.
passages.english: In the sixth [circle is] the star of Phaethon, which they call [the star of] Jupiter. Then in the highest heaven, that is, at the summit of the world, the star of Saturn is placed. Although it occupies the highest heaven and is loftier than all, its nature is nevertheless said to be cold, as Virgil confirms: "whither the cold star of Saturn withdraws itself."
passages.notes: "Pha et hontis" read as "Phaethontis" and "Jutis" as "Jovis". The sentence lacks a verb; "[circle is]" is supplied from the context.

passages.original: Bootes, stella est quæ Plaustrum, id est Septentrionem sequitur, qui eliam ab amiquis Arctophylax dicitur, sive minor Art tos. Unde et quidam eam Septentrionem dixerunt. Hanc spectant præcipue qui navigare noscuntur. De qua Lucanus : ....... Velox ubi nocte Bootes; Quae cum orta fuerit, cito facit occasum.
passages.english: Boötes is a star that follows the Wagon, that is, the Septentrio [the Great Bear]. It is also called Arctophylax by the ancients, or the Lesser Bear. Hence some have also called it Septentrio. Those who are known to sail watch it above all. Of it Lucan [says]: '....... where at night swift Boötes'. When it has risen, it quickly sets.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'eliam' for 'etiam', 'amiquis' for 'antiquis', 'Art tos' for 'Arctos'. The Lucan quotation is fragmentary, and the edition marks an omission with dots.

passages.original: 1Solet autem quaeri, ut ait sanctus Augustinus, utrum sol 42 et luna, et aliae stellae, corpora sola sint, an habeant rectores quosdam spirilus suos. Et si habent, utrum ab eis etiam vitaliter inspirentur, sicut animantur canes per animas animalium, an sola sine ulla permistione praesentia. Et dum motus alicujus corporis sine anima esse non possit, stellae, quae cum tanto ordine ac tanta ratione moventur, ut in nullo prorsus aliquando cursus earum impediatur, utrum animantes sint, et rationabiles videantur, non facile comprehendi potest.
passages.english: It is commonly asked, as Saint Augustine says, whether the sun and moon and the other stars are bodies only, or whether they have certain spirits of their own as their governors. And if they do have [them], [it is asked] whether they are also given life by them, as the bodies of animals are animated by the souls of animals, or whether [the spirits] are merely present without any mingling. And since the motion of any body cannot occur without a soul, it cannot easily be understood whether the stars, which move with such great order and such great reason that their course is never hindered in anything at all, are living beings, and whether they appear to be rational.
passages.notes: '42' is a page number and has been omitted. 'spirilus' is read as 'spiritus'. 'canes' (dogs) is evidently a corruption, probably of 'carnes' or 'corpora'. It has been translated as 'bodies'.

passages.original: 1. Ambrosium in libro Hexaemeron legi dicentem : < Quaeritur qualiter spatium aeris occupet umbra terrae efficiens nobis noctem , cum sol recedit a nobis diemque obducit, cum inferiora axis septentrionalis illuminat. Omne enim corpus umbram facit, et naturaliter umbra corpori adhaeret, adeo ut etiam pictores umbras corporum quae pinxerint nitantur exprimere, idque artis esse asserant non intermittere vim naturae.
passages.english: I have read Ambrose saying in his book Hexaemeron: 'It is asked how the shadow of the earth occupies the space of the air, producing night for us, when the sun withdraws from us and covers over the day, when it illuminates the lower parts of the northern axis. For every body casts a shadow, and the shadow naturally clings to the body, so much so that even painters strive to represent the shadows of the bodies they have painted, and they assert that it belongs to their art not to neglect the force of nature.
passages.notes: The quotation opened with '<' is not closed within the passage.

passages.original: Sed eorum sonitus tardius penetrat aures quam oculos splendor fulguris, ad instar securis arborem procul caedentis, cujus quidem ante cernis ictum quam ad aures perveniat sonitus. Ergo nubium attritu fulmina nascuntur. Nunquam enim sereno coelo fulgura micuerunt. Unde et Virgilius: Non alias coelo ceciderunt plura sereno Fulgura.
passages.english: But their sound reaches the ears more slowly than the brightness of the lightning reaches the eyes. It is like an axe cutting a tree far off: you see its stroke before the sound reaches your ears. Thunderbolts, therefore, arise from the friction of clouds. For lightning has never flashed from a clear sky. Hence Virgil also [says]: 'Never did more lightning fall from a clear sky.'
passages.notes: The text says 'never' (nunquam), but Virgil's line in fact describes lightning from a clear sky as a portent. The tension lies in the source.

passages.original: 4. Lucretius autem dicit fulmina ex minutis seminibus constare, ideo penetrabilia esse; ubicunque autem fulmen ceciderit, sulphuris odorem emittit. Virgilius: Et late circum loca sulphure fumant, Et Lucanus: Æthereoque nocens fumabit sulphure ferrum.
passages.english: 4. Lucretius, however, says that thunderbolts consist of minute seeds, and that they are therefore able to penetrate. Wherever a thunderbolt has fallen, it gives off a smell of sulphur. Virgil [says]: 'And the places far around smoke with sulphur'. And Lucan [says]: 'And the harmful iron will smoke with heavenly sulphur.'

passages.original: Notandum est ex libro Job, quod cogitur aer iste visibilis, ut conglobetur ; conglobatus autem in nubes vertitur. Sic ipse dicit: Subito aer cogitur in nubibus, et ventus transiens fugabit eas (Job. XXXVII, 21.) Et Virgilius :
passages.english: It should be noted from the book of Job that this visible air is compressed so that it gathers into a mass, and once gathered it turns into clouds. So he himself says: 'Suddenly the air is compressed into clouds, and a passing wind will drive them away' (Job 37:21). And Virgil [says]:
passages.notes: The Virgil quotation is missing from the passage.

passages.original: 1. Ait Ambrosius quod plerumque glacialibus ventorum natibus rigentes aquae solidanlur in nivem, et rupto aere nix funditur.
passages.english: 1. Ambrose says that very often waters, stiffened by icy blasts of the winds, are solidified into snow, and when the air is broken the snow is poured out.
passages.notes: 'natibus' and 'solidanlur' are read as 'flatibus' and 'solidantur'.

passages.original: 1. Ventus est aer commotus et agitatus, approbante Lucretio : Ventus enim fit ubi est agitando percitus aer. Quod etiam in loco tranquillissimo et ab omnibus ventis quieto brevi flabello approbari potest, quo etiam muscas abigentes aerem commovemus, flaturaque sentimus. Quod cum evenerit occultiori quodam motu coelestium vel terrenorum corporum per magnum spatium mundi ventus vocatur ex diversis partibus coeli nomina etiam diversa sortitus.
passages.english: 1. Wind is air moved and stirred, as Lucretius confirms: 'For wind arises when the air is roused by stirring.' This can be shown even in a very calm place, still from all winds, with a small fan. With [a fan] we also move the air when driving away flies, and we feel the breezes. When this happens through some more hidden motion of heavenly or earthly bodies across the great space of the world, it is called wind, and it has also received different names from the different parts of the sky.
passages.notes: 'flaturaque' is read as 'flatusque' (breezes).

passages.original: 2. Item Yarro dicit signum esse tempestatis, dum de parte Aquilonis fulgurat, et dum de parte Euri intonat. Nigidius quoque ait: Luna si summo corniculo maculas nigras habuerit in primis partibus mensis, imbres fore ; si in medio, tunc cum plena sint in ea cornicula, serenitatem. Certe si rubet, quasi aurum, ventos ostendit.
passages.english: 2. Likewise Varro says that it is a sign of a storm when there is lightning from the direction of the north wind and thunder from the direction of the east wind. Nigidius also says: if the moon has black spots on the tip of its horn in the first part of the month, there will be rains; if [they are] in the middle, at the time when its horns are full, [there will be] fair weather. Certainly, if it is red like gold, it indicates winds.
passages.notes: "Yarro" is a scanning error for Varro.

passages.original: 53 3. Aratus autem dicit, si Aquilonium cornu lunæ sit correctius, Aquilonem imminere. Item si cornu Australe sit erectius, Notum imminere. Quarta autem luna futurarum index certissima habetur aurarum. Unde et Virgilius dicit: Sin ortu in quarlo, namque is certissimus auctor. Plura neque obtusis per coelum cornibus ibit. Tolus et. ille dies, et qui nascemur ab illis Exactum ad mensem pluvia, ventisque carebunt.
passages.english: 3. Aratus says that if the northern horn of the moon is more upright, the north wind is imminent. Likewise, if the southern horn is more upright, the south wind is imminent. The fourth moon is held to be the surest indicator of coming winds. Hence Virgil also says: 'But if at its fourth rising (for that is the surest guide) it travels through the sky clear and with horns not blunted, that whole day, and those born from it to the month's end, will be free of rain and winds.'
passages.notes: '53' is a page number and has been omitted. 'correctius' is read as 'erectius'. The quotation contains scanning errors: 'quarlo' (quarto), 'Plura' (Pura), 'Tolus' (Totus), 'nascemur' (nascentur). It has been translated as Virgil's evident sense.

passages.original: 4. Item idem Virgilius dicit : Si sol in ortu suo maculosus ait, atque sub nube latens, aut si dimidia parte apparuerit, imbres futuros. Item Varro ait: Si exoriens concavus videbitur, ita ut in medio fulgeat, et radios faciat partim ad Austrum, partim ad Aquilonem, tempestatem humidam et ventosam.
passages.english: 4. Likewise the same Virgil says: if the sun at its rising is spotted and hidden beneath a cloud, or if it appears with half [its disc], rains are coming. Likewise Varro says: if at its rising it appears hollow, so that it shines in the middle and sends out rays partly to the south, partly to the north, [it signals] a wet and windy storm.
passages.notes: "ait" in "maculosus ait" is evidently a misreading of "sit" and is translated so.

passages.original: 5. Item idem, Si sol, inquit, rubeat in occasu, sincerus fere dies erit: si palleat, tempestates significat. Nigidius quoque : Si pallidus, inquit, sol in nigras nubes occidat, Aquilonem ventum significat. Item Dominus in Evangelio: Si facto, inquit, vespere rubicundum fuerit coetum. mane serenum erit. Si mane rutilat triste cœ- lum, tempestas futura erit, et cum Auster ventus flaverit, æstus erit.
passages.english: 5. Likewise the same [author] says: if the sun is red at its setting, the day will be generally clear; if it is pale, it signifies storms. Nigidius also says: if the sun sets pale into black clouds, it signifies a north wind. Likewise the Lord in the Gospel says: "When evening has come, if the sky is red, the morning will be fair. If in the morning the sky glows red and gloomy, there will be a storm; and when the south wind blows, there will be heat."
passages.notes: "coetum" is read as "coelum" (sky).

passages.original: Sicque, naturalis ordins perturbata temperie, inficiuntur elementa, et fit corruptio aeris, et aura pestilens, et oritur pernicies, et corruptelæ vitium in homines, et cætera animantia. Unde et Virgilius : Corrupto coeli tractu miseraudaque venit, Arboribusque satisque lues.
passages.english: And so, when the balance of the natural order is disturbed, the elements are infected. A corruption of the air arises, and a pestilent breeze, and ruin springs up, and the vice of corruption [spreads] into human beings and the other living creatures. Hence Virgil also [says]: 'From a corrupted region of the sky there came a pitiable plague upon the trees and crops.'
passages.notes: 'ordins' and 'miseraudaque' are read as 'ordinis' and 'miserandaque'.

passages.original: Quod etiam Clemens discipulus apostolorum visus est indicare, cum dicit : Oceanus intransmeabilis est, et hi qui ultra eum sunt mundi. Philosophi autem aiunt quod post Oceanum terra nulla sit, sed solo denso aere Dubium contineatur 56 mare, sicut et terra subterius, ideo et Lucanus : Cum mare convolvit gentes, cum littora Thetys Noluit ulla pali cœlo contenta tenere, Tunc quoque tanta malis moles crevisset in astra, hi superum reclor pressisset nubibus uudas.
passages.english: Clement, the disciple of the apostles, also seems to have indicated this when he says: "The Ocean cannot be crossed, and [neither can] those worlds that are beyond it." The philosophers, however, say that beyond the Ocean there is no land, but that the sea is held up by dense air alone, just as the earth is from beneath. Hence Lucan too: "When the sea rolls over the nations, when Tethys refused to hold any shores, content with the sky of the pole, then too so great a mass would have grown to the stars from these evils, [and] the ruler of the gods would have pressed down the waves with clouds."
passages.notes: "Dubium" before "contineatur" and "56" appear to be marginal or page intrusions and are omitted. The Lucan quotation is garbled in this edition ("pali" read as "poli", "hi superum reclor" as "hic superum rector", "uudas" as "undas"), and its syntax is uncertain. The version of the Clement quotation is unclear: "and those worlds which are beyond it" may be the intended sense, without any implied verb.

passages.original: 1. Rursus Ambrosius doclor docuit dicens : Mare idcirco dicunt 57 veteres saltas, atque amaras habere aquas, pro eo quod ea quæ ex divertis fluviis in id influunt, solis ardore, ac ventorum flatibus absumantur, tantumque diurno vapore consumi, quantum p.r singulos dies ex omnibus amnium cursibus in ipsum invehitur.
passages.english: Again, Ambrose the teacher taught, saying: "The ancients say that the sea has salt and bitter waters for this reason: that what flows into it from various rivers is consumed by the heat of the sun and the blasts of the winds, and that as much is consumed by the daily evaporation as is carried into it each day from all the courses of the rivers."
passages.notes: Read "salsas" for "saltas", "diversis" for "divertis", "per" for "p.r"; "57" is a page mark.

passages.original: 3. Sinus majores recessus maris dicuntur, ut Caspius, Arabicus, Indicus. Minores autem anguli, ut Paestanus, Amyclanus, et cæteri similes. Flustra motus maris sine tempestate fluctuantis. Naevius in Bello Puuico sic ait : Onenariæ onustæ stabant in fluatris, ac si diceret in salo.
passages.english: 3. The larger recesses of the sea are called gulfs, such as the Caspian, the Arabian and the Indian; the smaller ones, however, [are called] corners, such as the Paestan, the Amyclan and others like them. *Flustra* is the motion of a sea heaving without a storm. Naevius in the *Punic War* says thus: "The laden cargo ships stood in the *flustra*," as if he were saying "in the swell."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "Puuico" for Punico, "Onenariæ" for Onerariae, "fluatris" for flustris.

passages.original: 4. Moles, quæ eminent, et procurrunt mari. De quibus Pacuvius : Omnes latebras sublata mole obtrusas. Sinus cæcus fluctus tumens, necdum tamen canus. De quo Alta in Togatis sic ait : 59 Pro populo fluctus cæcos faciunt per discordiam. Et Augustus, inquit, Nos venimus Neapolim fluctu quidem cæco.
passages.english: 4. Moles are [masses] that stand out and project into the sea. Of these Pacuvius [says]: "All hiding places blocked by the mole raised up." A blind wave is a swelling wave that is not yet white. Of this Atta in the *Togatae* says thus: "For the people they make blind waves through discord." And Augustus says: "We came to Naples on a blind wave indeed."
passages.notes: "Sinus cæcus" is presumably an error for "fluctus caecus" (blind wave), as the citations show. "Alta" is taken as Atta, an author of *togatae*. "59" is a page number and is omitted. The Pacuvius fragment is obscure.

passages.original: 5. Ditus, quidquid aqua alluit, Flumen omnis humor, qui vel modice fluit. Torrens fluvius, qui pluvia crescit, siccitate torreseit : de quo Pacuvius : Flammeo vapore torrens terræ. Ostia exitus fluminum in mare. Tollæ aquarum projectus, quales sunt in Aniene flumine quam maxime præcipites.
passages.english: 5. The shore is whatever the water washes. A stream is any liquid that flows, even a little. A torrent is a river that swells with rain and dries up in drought; of it Pacuvius [says]: "a torrent of the earth with fiery heat." Mouths are the outlets of rivers into the sea. *Tollae* are the outflows of waters, such as are especially steep on the river Anio.
passages.notes: "Ditus" is read as "Litus" (shore) and "torreseit" as "torrescit". "Tollae" is a rare term for cascades; its sense is uncertain. The Pacuvius fragment is obscure.

passages.original: 1. Qualiter terra super aerem fundata libratis credatur stare ponderibus, sic dicit Ambrosius : « De ferræ autem qualitate, sive positione sufliciat secundum Scripturam Job sciendum quia suspendit terram in nihilo. > Philosophi quoque similiter opinantur, aere denso terram sustineri, et quasi spongiam mole sua immobilem pendere, sicque, ut aequali motu hinc atque inde, veluti alarum suffulta remigiis, ex omni parte librata propendeat, nec in partem possint inclinari alteram.
passages.english: On how the earth, founded upon air, is believed to stand with balanced weights, Ambrose speaks thus: "Concerning the nature or position of the earth, let it suffice to know, according to the Scripture of Job, that he hangs the earth upon nothing." The philosophers too hold a similar opinion: that the earth is supported by dense air and hangs immovable by its own mass, like a sponge, and thus that, with equal motion on this side and that, as if borne up by the oarage of wings, it hangs balanced on every side and cannot be tilted toward one side or the other.
passages.notes: Read "terrae" for "ferræ", "sufficiat" for "sufliciat". The sense of "quasi spongiam" in this context is uncertain.

passages.original: Unde et Sallustlius : Venti, inquit, per cata terræ præcipitati, rupti aliquot montes, tumulique sedere. Ergo, ut diximus, tremor terrae, vel spiritu venti per cava terrae, vel ruina inferiorum, motuque undae existit. Sic enim et Lucanus ait : Terraque dehiscente Insolitis..... tremuerunt motibus Alpes.
passages.english: Hence Sallust too says: "Winds rushing headlong through the hollows of the earth, some mountains were burst open, and hills sank down." Therefore, as we have said, a trembling of the earth arises either from the breath of wind through the hollows of the earth, or from the collapse of lower parts and the motion of water. For so Lucan also says: "And with the earth gaping open [...] the Alps trembled with unaccustomed motions."
passages.notes: Read "cava" for "cata". The Lucan quotation has a gap marked in the edition.

passages.original: Asiam autem, et Libyam cum Ægypto disterminat ostium Nili fluvii, quod Canopicum appellatur. Asiam ab Europa Tanais dividitbifariam se conjiciens in paludem, quae Mæotis appellatur. Asia autem, ut ait beatissimus Augustinus, a meridie per orientem usque ad septentrionem pervenit. Europa vero a septentrione usque ad occidentem, atque inde Africa ab occidente usque ad meridiem.
passages.english: Asia, moreover, is separated from Libya together with Egypt by the mouth of the river Nile that is called the Canopic. The Tanais divides Asia from Europe, throwing itself in two branches into the marsh that is called Maeotis. Asia, as the most blessed Augustine says, extends from the south through the east as far as the north; Europe from the north as far as the west; and then Africa from the west as far as the south.
passages.notes: "dividitbifariam" is read as "dividit bifariam". The Tanais is the Don, and Maeotis is the Sea of Azov.
